opcodes.name: invoke-virtual/range

operands.name: AA
operands.description: AA (8 bits): argument word count, 0–255; smali derives it from the range.

operands.name: vCCCC
operands.description: CCCC (16 bits): first argument register, v0–v65535.

operands.name: vNNNN
operands.description: Not encoded: last argument register, NNNN = CCCC + AA - 1.

operands.name: Lclass;->method(params)ret
operands.description: BBBB (16 bits): method_ids index (meth@BBBB).

opcodes.summary: Call a virtual method, dispatched on the receiver's runtime class, with arguments in a register range.
opcodes.description: invoke-virtual/range is the range form of invoke-virtual: the arguments are a run of consecutive registers instead of an explicit list. Compilers use it when a call needs more than five argument words or when the arguments sit above v15. The call semantics are identical to invoke-virtual.

Throws NullPointerException for a null receiver; resolution can throw NoSuchMethodError, IncompatibleClassChangeError (static or interface method) or IllegalAccessError; AbstractMethodError if the selected method is abstract. commonMistakes: Listing registers that are not consecutive: {v0 .. v5} means exactly v0, v1, v2, v3, v4, v5.

Using invoke-virtual for a private method or constructor (use invoke-direct) or for an interface method (use invoke-interface).

opcodes.summary: Call the superclass's (or a default interface) implementation of a method, with arguments in a register range.
opcodes.description: invoke-super/range is the range form of invoke-super: the arguments are a run of consecutive registers instead of an explicit list. opcodes.name: neg-int

operands.name: vA
operands.description: A (4 bits): destination register, v0–v15.

operands.name: vB
operands.description: B (4 bits): source register, v0–v15.

    neg-int v0, p0
    return v0
.end method

Using registers above v15: move the value to a low register first.
Using the int variant on a register pair: the type must match exactly.

    return v0
.end method

opcodes.name: invoke-polymorphic

operands.name: A
operands.description: A (4 bits): argument word count, 1–5 (the receiver is always present).

operands.name: vC
operands.description: C (4 bits): the receiver: the MethodHandle (or VarHandle) object.

operands.name: vD
operands.description: D (4 bits): first argument register.

operands.name: vE
operands.description: E (4 bits): second argument register.

operands.name: vF
operands.description: F (4 bits): third argument register.

operands.name: vG
operands.description: G (4 bits): fourth argument register.

operands.name: Lclass;->method(params)ret
operands.description: BBBB (16 bits): method_ids index (meth@BBBB) of the signature-polymorphic method, e.g. MethodHandle.invokeExact.

operands.name: (params)ret
operands.description: HHHH (16 bits): proto_ids index (proto@HHHH): the actual argument types and the expected return type at this call site.

opcodes.summary: Invoke a signature-polymorphic method such as MethodHandle.invokeExact.
opcodes.description: invoke-polymorphic calls methods like MethodHandle.invokeExact, whose declared signature is just a placeholder: each call site supplies its own argument and return types. The second reference, a prototype, records those types. Any result is collected with move-result*, as for other invokes.
opcodes.technical: Format 45cc (A|G|op BBBB F|E|D|C HHHH): 4 16-bit code units (8 bytes). vC is the receiver (the handle); vD..vG are the arguments. The method reference must name a signature-polymorphic method, and the proto describes the types actually passed and expected back. Exceptions are those of the invoked method: for invokeExact a type mismatch throws WrongMethodTypeException, a null receiver throws NullPointerException, and anything the target throws propagates. The instruction formats page lists only A = 1..5 for 45cc.
opcodes.example:
# int len = (int) lengthHandle.invokeExact("hello");
.method public static callLength(Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodHandle;)I
    .locals 1
    const-string v0, "hello"
    invoke-polymorphic {p0, v0}, Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodHandle;->invokeExact([Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;, (Ljava/lang/String;)I
    move-result v0
    return v0
.end method
opcodes.exampleExplanation: The method reference is always invokeExact([Object)Object, but the proto (Ljava/lang/String;)I says this call passes one String and expects an int back, so move-result (not move-result-object) collects the result.
opcodes.registerUsage: Reads the receiver vC and up to four argument registers (v0–v15 each). The result, if any, is collected with move-result*. Remember that pN registers are aliases for the last registers of the frame: in a method with many locals, p0 may be v20 or higher and then cannot be named by a 4-bit register field.
opcodes.compatibility: Requires dex version 038 or later; the dex format documentation says support for 038 was added in Android 8.0 (API 26). Assemble with smali --api 26 or higher; older devices refuse to load such a dex file. invoke-polymorphic is only valid for signature-polymorphic methods: MethodHandle.invoke and MethodHandle.invokeExact, and the VarHandle accessor methods (get, set, compareAndSet, ...). java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle is in the public SDK from API 26; VarHandle from API 33.
commonMistakes: Using it for an ordinary method: only signature-polymorphic methods are allowed; everything else uses invoke-virtual.
Writing a proto that doesn't match the handle's type exactly when calling invokeExact: the call throws WrongMethodTypeException.
Choosing the move-result variant from the method reference's return type (Object) instead of the proto's return type.
Assembling for an API level below 26: the dex version must be 038 or later.

opcodes.name: invoke-custom
opcodes.syntax: invoke-custom {vC, vD, vE, vF, vG}, call_site_0("name", (params)ret, extraArgs...)@Lbootstrap/Class;->bootstrap(Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodHandles$Lookup;Ljava/lang/String;Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodType;...)Ljava/lang/invoke/CallSite;

operands.name: A
operands.description: A (4 bits): argument word count, 0–5.

operands.name: vC
operands.description: C (4 bits): first argument register.

operands.name: vD
operands.description: D (4 bits): second argument register.

operands.name: vE
operands.description: E (4 bits): third argument register.

operands.name: vF
operands.description: F (4 bits): fourth argument register.

operands.name: vG
operands.description: G (4 bits): fifth argument register.

operands.name: call_site
operands.description: BBBB (16 bits): call_site_ids index (call_site@BBBB). smali writes it as name("methodName", (proto), extra args...)@bootstrapMethod.

opcodes.summary: Resolve a call site through its bootstrap method and invoke its target (invokedynamic).
opcodes.description: invoke-custom is Dalvik's counterpart of the JVM's invokedynamic. The first time it runs, a bootstrap method decides what the call site should do and returns a CallSite. Every execution then calls that CallSite's target method handle with the given arguments.
opcodes.technical: Format 35c (A|G|op BBBB F|E|D|C): 3 16-bit code units (6 bytes). The instruction runs in two phases. Call site resolution: if the call site has no associated java.lang.invoke.CallSite yet, its bootstrap linker method is invoked with the arguments stored in the dex file's call_site_item; the CallSite it returns becomes associated with the call site, unless another thread got there first, in which case the first association wins. Call site invocation: the CallSite's target MethodHandle is invoked as if by invoke-polymorphic (an exact invocation) with the instruction's argument registers. Exceptions from the bootstrap method are wrapped in BootstrapMethodError, which is also thrown when the bootstrap method doesn't return a CallSite, the CallSite's target is null, or the target has the wrong type. The result, if any, is retrieved with move-result*.
opcodes.exampleExplanation: On first execution Bootstraps.link receives the lookup, the name "combine" and the type (II)I and returns a CallSite; the target is then invoked with p0 and p1, and the int result is read with move-result.
opcodes.javaEquivalent: // no direct Java syntax: emitted for invokedynamic call sites (e.g. lambdas or string concatenation when they are not desugared)
opcodes.registerUsage: Reads up to five argument registers (v0–v15). Writes no register directly; the result, if any, is collected with move-result*.
opcodes.compatibility: Requires dex version 038 or later; the dex format documentation says support for 038 was added in Android 8.0 (API 26). Assemble with smali --api 26 or higher; older devices refuse to load such a dex file. invoke-custom is rare in typical app code because D8 usually desugars invokedynamic (lambdas, string concatenation) into ordinary classes and calls.
commonMistakes: Expecting a receiver: invoke-custom has no implicit this; all registers are arguments matching the call site's method type.
Writing a bootstrap method that returns null or a CallSite of the wrong type, which leads to BootstrapMethodError.
Assuming the bootstrap method runs on every call: it runs once, when the call site is first resolved.
Assembling for an API level below 26: requires dex 038.

opcodes.name: invoke-custom/range

operands.name: AA
operands.description: AA (8 bits): argument word count, 0–255.

operands.name: vCCCC
operands.description: CCCC (16 bits): first argument register, v0–v65535.

operands.name: vNNNN
operands.description: Not encoded: last argument register, NNNN = CCCC + AA - 1.

operands.name: call_site
operands.description: BBBB (16 bits): call_site_ids index (call_site@BBBB).

opcodes.summary: invoke-custom with its arguments taken from a consecutive register range.
opcodes.description: This is the range form of invoke-custom. The call site is resolved and invoked in exactly the same way, but the arguments come from consecutive registers, so you can pass more than five words or use high registers.
opcodes.technical: Format 3rc (AA|op BBBB CCCC): 3 16-bit code units (6 bytes). The instruction runs in two phases. Call site resolution: if the call site has no associated java.lang.invoke.CallSite yet, its bootstrap linker method is invoked with the arguments stored in the dex file's call_site_item; the CallSite it returns becomes associated with the call site, unless another thread got there first, in which case the first association wins. Call site invocation: the CallSite's target MethodHandle is invoked as if by invoke-polymorphic (an exact invocation) with the instruction's argument registers. Exceptions from the bootstrap method are wrapped in BootstrapMethodError, which is also thrown when the bootstrap method doesn't return a CallSite, the CallSite's target is null, or the target has the wrong type. Arguments are read from vCCCC..vCCCC+AA-1.
opcodes.example:
invoke-custom/range {v16 .. v17}, call_site_1("combine", (II)I)@Lcom/acme/demo/Bootstraps;->link(Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodHandles$Lookup;Ljava/lang/String;Ljava/lang/invoke/MethodType;)Ljava/lang/invoke/CallSite;
move-result v0
opcodes.exampleExplanation: The two int arguments live in v16 and v17, beyond 4-bit register reach, so the range form is used.
opcodes.javaEquivalent: // no direct Java syntax (invokedynamic call site)
opcodes.registerUsage: Reads vCCCC..vNNNN (consecutive). The result, if any, is collected with move-result*.
opcodes.compatibility: Requires dex version 038 or later; the dex format documentation says support for 038 was added in Android 8.0 (API 26). Assemble with smali --api 26 or higher; older devices refuse to load such a dex file. invoke-custom is rare in typical app code because D8 usually desugars invokedynamic (lambdas, string concatenation) into ordinary classes and calls.
commonMistakes: Using non-consecutive registers.
Miscounting words for long/double arguments.
Assembling for an API level below 26.

opcodes.name: const-method-handle

operands.name: vAA
operands.description: AA (8 bits): destination register, v0–v255; receives a java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle.

operands.name: kind@member
operands.description: BBBB (16 bits): method_handles index (method_handle@BBBB). smali writes the handle type and member, e.g. invoke-static@Lfoo;->bar()V or static-get@Lfoo;->FIELD:I.

opcodes.summary: Load a MethodHandle constant from the dex method_handles table into vAA.
opcodes.description: const-method-handle loads a ready-made MethodHandle for a method or field accessor that the dex file declares as a constant. It is the counterpart of loading a method handle constant from the class-file constant pool. Code can then call the handle with invoke-polymorphic.
opcodes.technical: Format 21c (AA|op BBBB): 2 16-bit code units (4 bytes). The method_handle_item gives the handle type (static-put, static-get, instance-put, instance-get, invoke-static, invoke-instance, invoke-constructor, invoke-direct or invoke-interface) and the field or method it refers to. Resolving the handle can throw linkage errors, for example when the member doesn't exist or isn't accessible.
opcodes.exampleExplanation: v0 receives a handle to Integer.toString(int), which is then called exactly with 42; the String result lands in v2.
opcodes.javaEquivalent: // closest Java (runtime lookup, not a constant): MethodHandles.lookup().findStatic(Integer.class, "toString", MethodType.methodType(String.class, int.class))
opcodes.registerUsage: Writes vAA (v0–v255).
opcodes.compatibility: Requires dex version 039 or later; the dex format documentation says support for 039 was added in Android 9.0 (API 28). Assemble with smali --api 28 or higher; older devices refuse to load such a dex file. java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle itself is in the public SDK from API 26.
commonMistakes: Assembling for an API level below 28: requires dex 039.
Picking the wrong handle kind (e.g. invoke-instance for a static method), which fails resolution.
Calling the handle with invoke-virtual instead of invoke-polymorphic.

opcodes.name: const-method-type

operands.name: vAA
operands.description: AA (8 bits): destination register, v0–v255; receives a java.lang.invoke.MethodType.

operands.name: (params)ret
operands.description: BBBB (16 bits): proto_ids index (proto@BBBB) of the method prototype, e.g. (ILjava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String;.

opcodes.summary: Load a MethodType constant for a method prototype into vAA.
opcodes.description: const-method-type turns a method prototype from the dex file into a java.lang.invoke.MethodType object. MethodType values describe the parameter and return types of method handles, for example to check or adapt a handle's type.
opcodes.technical: Format 21c (AA|op BBBB): 2 16-bit code units (4 bytes). Resolves the proto_id at proto@BBBB and writes the MethodType reference to vAA. Resolution can throw linkage errors (such as NoClassDefFoundError) if a type in the prototype cannot be resolved.
opcodes.exampleExplanation: The MethodType (int, String) -> String is loaded as a constant and used to adapt the handle in p1.
opcodes.kotlinEquivalent: val t = MethodType.methodType(String::class.java, Int::class.java, String::class.java)   // Int::class.java is int.class
opcodes.registerUsage: Writes vAA (v0–v255).
opcodes.compatibility: Requires dex version 039 or later; the dex format documentation says support for 039 was added in Android 9.0 (API 28). Assemble with smali --api 28 or higher; older devices refuse to load such a dex file. java.lang.invoke.MethodType is part of the java.lang.invoke API available from API 26.
commonMistakes: Assembling for an API level below 28: requires dex 039.
Writing the prototype with dotted class names instead of descriptors.
Confusing it with const-class: the result is a MethodType, not a Class.

opcodes.name: packed-switch-payload

operands.name: ident
operands.description: ushort = 0x0100: identifying pseudo-opcode

operands.name: size
operands.description: ushort: number of entries in the table

operands.name: first_key
operands.description: int: first (and lowest) switch case value

operands.name: targets
operands.description: int[]: list of size relative branch targets. The targets are relative to the address of the switch opcode, not of this table.

opcodes.summary: Data table for packed-switch: a first key followed by consecutive branch targets.
opcodes.description: This pseudo-instruction is not executed; it is the jump table that packed-switch reads. It stores the lowest case value and one branch target for each consecutive value after it. In smali you write it as a .packed-switch ... .end packed-switch block, usually at the end of the method.
opcodes.technical: Layout: ushort ident = 0x0100, ushort size, int first_key, int targets[size]. Each target is a signed code-unit offset relative to the address of the packed-switch instruction that uses the table, not to the table itself. The table must start on a 4-byte boundary (an even code-unit offset), so a nop may be inserted before it, and it must never be reached by normal execution. Total size: (size * 2) + 4 code units.
opcodes.example:
.method public static label(I)Ljava/lang/String;
    .locals 1
    packed-switch p0, :pswitch_data_0
    const-string v0, "other"
    return-object v0

    :pswitch_0
    const-string v0, "zero"
    return-object v0

    :pswitch_1
    const-string v0, "one"
    return-object v0

    :pswitch_2
    const-string v0, "two"
    return-object v0

    :pswitch_data_0
    .packed-switch 0x0
        :pswitch_0
        :pswitch_1
        :pswitch_2
    .end packed-switch
.end method
opcodes.exampleExplanation: The block after :pswitch_data_0 is the payload. 0x0 is first_key and the three labels are the targets for the values 0, 1 and 2.
opcodes.registerUsage: None. Payloads are data tables, not executable instructions, and touch no registers.
opcodes.compatibility: Part of the original instruction set: valid in every dex version (035 and later) on all Android releases (API 1+).
commonMistakes: Placing the payload where execution can fall into it (for example before a return): it must be unreachable data.
Computing targets relative to the table: they are relative to the switch instruction.
Sharing one payload between two packed-switch instructions; smali requires one table per switch.

opcodes.name: sparse-switch-payload

operands.name: ident
operands.description: ushort = 0x0200: identifying pseudo-opcode

operands.name: size
operands.description: ushort: number of entries in the table

operands.name: keys
operands.description: int[]: list of size key values, sorted low-to-high

operands.name: targets
operands.description: int[]: list of size relative branch targets, each corresponding to the key value at the same index. The targets are relative to the address of the switch opcode, not of this table.

opcodes.summary: Data table for sparse-switch: sorted keys and a branch target for each key.
opcodes.description: This pseudo-instruction holds the case table of a sparse-switch: every case key with its own branch target. The keys are kept sorted so that the runtime can search them quickly. In smali it is a .sparse-switch block of key -> :label lines.
opcodes.technical: Layout: ushort ident = 0x0200, ushort size, int keys[size] sorted low-to-high, int targets[size]. Each target is a signed code-unit offset relative to the sparse-switch instruction. The table must be 4-byte aligned and must not be reachable by normal execution. Total size: (size * 4) + 2 code units.
opcodes.example:
.method public static statusText(I)Ljava/lang/String;
    .locals 1
    sparse-switch p0, :sswitch_data_0
    const-string v0, "unknown"
    return-object v0

    :sswitch_0
    const-string v0, "OK"
    return-object v0

    :sswitch_1
    const-string v0, "Not Found"
    return-object v0

    :sswitch_2
    const-string v0, "Server Error"
    return-object v0

    :sswitch_data_0
    .sparse-switch
        0xc8 -> :sswitch_0
        0x194 -> :sswitch_1
        0x1f4 -> :sswitch_2
    .end sparse-switch
.end method
opcodes.exampleExplanation: The .sparse-switch block is the payload: three sorted keys (200, 404, 500), each mapped to the label of its case.
opcodes.registerUsage: None. Payloads are data tables, not executable instructions, and touch no registers.
opcodes.compatibility: Part of the original instruction set: valid in every dex version (035 and later) on all Android releases (API 1+).
commonMistakes: Listing keys in unsorted order or with duplicates.
Treating it as a packed table: entries are explicit key/target pairs, not offsets from a first key.
Letting execution fall into the table.

opcodes.name: fill-array-data-payload

operands.name: ident
operands.description: ushort = 0x0300: identifying pseudo-opcode

operands.name: element_width
operands.description: ushort: number of bytes in each element

operands.name: size
operands.description: uint: number of elements in the table

operands.name: data
operands.description: ubyte[]: data values

opcodes.summary: Data table for fill-array-data: element width, element count and the raw element bytes.
opcodes.description: This pseudo-instruction holds the constant values that fill-array-data copies into a primitive array. It records how many bytes each element takes and how many elements there are, followed by the raw data. smali writes it as an .array-data block; dexlib2 calls it array-payload internally.
opcodes.technical: Layout: ushort ident = 0x0300, ushort element_width (bytes per element), uint size (number of elements), ubyte data[size * element_width], stored little-endian. smali accepts widths 1, 2, 4 and 8 (byte/boolean, short/char, int/float, long/double). The table must be 4-byte aligned and unreachable by normal execution; an odd total byte count is padded to whole code units. Total size: (size * element_width + 1) / 2 + 4 code units.
opcodes.example:
.method public static weights()[S
    .locals 1
    const/4 v0, 0x3
    new-array v0, v0, [S
    fill-array-data v0, :array_0
    return-object v0

    :array_0
    .array-data 2
        0xas
        0x14s
        0x1es
    .end array-data
.end method
opcodes.exampleExplanation: The .array-data 2 block is a payload with element_width 2 (short) and three elements: 10, 20 and 30. The s suffix marks short literals.
opcodes.registerUsage: None. Payloads are data tables, not executable instructions, and touch no registers.
opcodes.compatibility: Part of the original instruction set: valid in every dex version (035 and later) on all Android releases (API 1+).
commonMistakes: Choosing an element width that doesn't match the array type, so the values are rejected or land in the wrong slots.
Expecting it to work for String[] or other object arrays: only primitive arrays can be filled.
Letting execution fall into the table.
